C0.r: **Frazer Golden Bough, III (Taboo and the Perils of the Soul), London 1914.
C0.p: A taboo forbidding contact with the supernatural, so that a person must not touch or deal with spirits or otherworldly powers.

C10.r: *Halliday in Penzer VIII xiv; BP II 63 n. 1.—N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 338 n. 217a; India: Thompson-Balys.
C10.p: A taboo against profanely calling up a spirit, such as the devil, by irreverent means.

C10.1.p: The practice of Druidism is forbidden under taboo.

C11.r: Halm Aesop No. 90; Wienert FFC LVI 81 (ET 468, 469), 109 (ST 212, cf. ST 109, 115, 141, 342); *Jacobs Aesop 216 No. 69; *BP III 294; Italian Novella: Rotunda; U.S.: Baughman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
C11.p: A weary old man, tired of life, summons Death; when Death comes, the old man asks it to help him with his load instead of taking him.

C12.p: The devil is invoked and appears suddenly and unexpectedly when someone calls on him.

C12.1.r: Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 23; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 123 No. 47; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 41 No. 47; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 42 No. 25; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
C12.1.p: A person calls on the devil for help, and when the devil appears the man makes excuses to get away from him.

C12.1.1.p: A man who wants to become a magician is frightened when the helper spirit he has summoned actually appears. He had called on the devil for help.

C12.2.r: .. “ Devil does.—Type 821A; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 807.—Norwegian: Christiansen Norske Eventyr 105; Irish: Beal XXI 316; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 641.
C12.2.p: A person swears an oath invoking the devil to take him if what he says is untrue, a kind of curse that is taboo to speak.

C12.3.p: A person swears by wishing the devil would sharpen his scythe, and the devil takes the scythe away, leaving only the handle.

C12.4.p: A man entrusts his wife to the devil's care before leaving her. The devil takes the charge seriously and guards her chastity while the husband is away.

C12.4.1.p: A mother angrily wishes that her lazy daughter would marry the devil. The devil appears and marries her.

C12.5.r: Appears. Alphabet No. 246.—Esthonian: Aarne FFC XXV 120 No. 32; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 40 No. 32.
C12.5.p: A person uses the devil's name in a curse, which brings the devil into the situation unexpectedly.

C12.5.1.p: Noah's wife refuses to let the devil into the ark, and the devil tricks her into keeping the door shut. Noah finally loses patience and calls the devil in, and the devil enters as a mouse.

C12.5.2.p: A man curses in anger, and the devil grants the wish by taking away a stone.

C12.5.3.p: A girl who loves dancing uses the devil's name in her speech, and this brings the devil to her.

C12.5.4.p: A lost parson says he would rather have the devil as a guide than the clerk who is with him. The devil appears and causes the death of both men.

C12.5.5.p: A man angry at his wife calls on the devil to come down the chimney. The devil comes and makes the pudding black.

C12.5.6.p: A man swears he will punish the devil for poaching. The devil appears, the man runs away, and the devil carries off the man's wife instead.

C12.5.7.p: A wife curses her wicked husband, saying may the devil take him. The devil does take him.

C12.5.8.r: Origin of place name: En Spuyten Duyvil. U.S.: Baughman.
C12.5.8.p: A man swears he will cross the water regardless of the devil, and the devil takes him for using his name in that curse.

C13.r: *Type 470; **D.E. MacKay The Double Invitation in the Legend of Don Juan; *BP III 483 n. 1; *Wesselski Märchen 241 No. 51; Armeto La Leyenda de Don Juan (Madrid, 1908); *DeCock Studien en Essays 108—152, 308ff.; *Lancaster PMLA XXXVIII 471 n. 1; G. de Bevotte La Legende de Don Juan (Paris, 1906) (bibliography pp. 517—521); Manning PMLA XXXVIII 479; *Waxman JAFL XXI 184; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) no. 561; *Fb “menneskehoved” I 579b; Hartland Science 167; Sébillot France IV 132; Klapper Erzählungen des Mittelalters 157 No. 164; Gering Islenzk Aeventyri I 97 No. 34.
C13.p: A skull or statue is invited to dinner by a man who mocks it. The offended skull comes to the dinner and carries the host off to the other world.

C13.1.p: A prince invites an angel to his wedding, and the angel takes him away to the other world.

C14.p: A king says he has heard people speak of adversity but has never seen it. Someone summons the spirit of adversity, and it appears before him.

C15.p: A person wishes for a supernatural husband or wife, and the wish comes true.

C15.1.r: *Thompson The Star-Husband Tale (Studia Septentrionalia IV [1953] 93ff.); N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 330 n. 193.
C15.1.p: A person wishes for a husband who is a star, and the wish is granted.

C15.1.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 40, 43, (Sherente): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (1) 516.
C15.1.1.p: A person wishes for a wife who is a star, and the wish is granted.

C15.2.p: A person wishes for a tree as a husband, and the wish is granted. The tree comes to life as a man.

C16.p: A taboo that is broken by profanely calling up the spirits of the dead, causing them to be offended and to act against the person.

C20.p: A taboo that is broken by calling on an ogre or a destructive animal, which then comes to harm the person.

C21.r: He appears. Köhler-Bolte I 557; Köhler Zs. f. Vksk. VI 68; *Cosquin Études Folkloriques 532ff.
C21.p: A taboo in which uttering an exclamation of distress that includes the ogre's name summons the ogre.

C25.p: A man urging on his horses by threatening them with a bear, calling them 'bear's food'; the bear hears and comes after them.

C25.1.r: Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 321 No. 72, 323 No. 131; Japanese: Ikeda.
C25.1.p: A child is threatened with an ogre, and the ogre comes and carries the child away.

C26.r: (Cf. C15.)—*Type 552.—Norwegian: Christiansen Norske Eventyr 80.—N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 341 n. 231.
C26.p: A girl says she will marry a certain animal, and that animal appears and carries her off as her husband.

C30.p: A taboo broken by offending a supernatural relative, such as a spirit or otherworldly family member.

C31.r: *Hoffman-Krayer Zs. f. Vksk. XXV 120 n. 4; Irish myth: Cross; English: Child I 21, 485a, II 496b, 509a, IV 440b; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 340 n. 223a; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas VAM XV 180; Maori: Dixon 58, 72.
C31.p: A supernatural wife is offended by a slight and leaves to return to her old home.

C31.1.p: A taboo against looking at a supernatural wife; looking at her breaks the taboo.

C31.1.1.r: *BP III 114 (Gr. No. 137).—Middle English romance: Wells 145 (Parthenope of Blois).
C31.1.1.p: A taboo against looking at a supernatural wife too soon, before the appointed time.

C31.1.2.r: (Mélusine). The husband must not see the wife when she is transformed to an animal.—*Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXV (1933) 121; *Köhler-Bolte III 265nn. 1, 2; **Köhler Der Ursprung der Melusinensage (1895); Desaivre Le Mythe de la Mére Lusine (Extrait des Memoires de la Société de Statistique, Sciences, Lettres, et Arts de Deux-Sèvres [Saint-Maixent 1883]); Keightley Fairy Mythology 480; Baring-Gould Curious Myths 470; Hartland Science 201; Holmström Studier över Svanjungfrumotivet 100; M. Nowack Die Melusinensage (Diss. 1886); *Fränkel Zs. f. Vksk. IV 387; Jegerlehner Oberwallis 307 No. 24.
C31.1.2.p: A taboo against looking at a supernatural wife on a certain occasion.

C31.1.3.p: A taboo against a man looking at his supernatural wife when she is naked.

C31.1.4.p: A taboo against a husband looking at his supernatural wife while she is giving birth.

C31.1.5.r: S. Am. Indian (Camacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 48.
C31.1.5.p: A taboo against opening the gourd in which a star-wife is kept; when curious girls open it, she flies up to the sky.

C31.2.r: (Cf. C33.1, C35.1.)—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 296 No. 21; Fjort: Dennett 44 No. 6; Indonesian: De Vries Volksverhalen I No. 35 n.
C31.2.p: A taboo against mentioning where a supernatural wife came from.

C31.3.r: Congo: Weeks 206f. No. 3; Fjort: Dennett 41 No. 5.—India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: De Vries Volksverhalen I No. 35 n.
C31.3.p: A taboo broken when a man disobeys his supernatural wife.

C31.4.r: *Chauvin VI 182 No. 343.—Greek: Fox 122 (Thetis).—Indonesian: De Vries Volksverhalen I No. 35 n.
C31.4.p: A taboo broken when a man blames his supernatural wife.

C31.4.1.r: Hindu: Penzer VII 21 n. 3, II 252f.; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: De Vries Volksverhalen I No. 35 n.
C31.4.1.p: A taboo broken when a man questions his supernatural wife.

C31.4.2.r: English: Child V 495 s.v. “scolding”.—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 296 No. 21; England: Baughman.—Melanesian: Codrington The Melanesians 172.
C31.4.2.p: A taboo broken when a man scolds his supernatural wife.

C31.5.r: *BP II 327; Köhler-Bolte I 308ff.—Irish myth: Cross; English: Wells 132 (Sir Launfal). Fjort: Dennett 42 No. 6.
C31.5.p: A taboo broken when a man boasts of his supernatural wife.

C31.6.r: *Type 400; BP II 318ff. (Gr. No. 92); ‘Fb “ønske” III 1179a.—English: Wells 132 (Sir Launfal.)
C31.6.p: A person must not call out to or summon their supernatural wife; doing so breaks the taboo and brings punishment or loss.

C31.7.r: Indonesian: De Vries Volksverhalen I No. 35 n.
C31.7.p: A person must not louse, that is pick lice from the head of, their supernatural wife; doing so breaks the taboo.

C31.8.r: Irish myth: Cross; Wales: Baughman; Kassai (Congo): Frobenius Atlantis XII 106.
C31.8.p: A person must not strike their supernatural wife; hitting her breaks the taboo.

C31.9.r: (Cf. C420). *Schofield PMLA XV 165; Irish myth: Cross.
C31.9.p: A person must not reveal the secrets of their supernatural wife; telling them breaks the taboo.

C31.10.p: A person must not give back to a divine or supernatural wife the garment that belongs to her; doing so breaks the taboo and she leaves or is lost.

C31.11.p: A person must not reproach their supernatural wife about her sisters; criticizing them breaks the taboo.

C31.12.p: A husband who is unfaithful to his supernatural wife loses her, as she is magical and leaves him.

C32.r: (Cf. C36.)—*Type 425; BP II 245ff. (Gr. No. 88).—India: *Thompson-Balys; S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 91.
C32.p: A broader taboo in which a person offends against their supernatural husband by breaking a prohibition set by him.

C32.1.r: *Type 425a; *BP II 234, 245ff., 266ff.; *Tegethoff Studien zum Märchentypus von Amor und Psyche 32; *Lang Cupid and Psyche (1886); *Fb “lys” II 483a.—India: Thompson-Balys.
C32.1.p: A wife must not look at her supernatural husband; looking at him breaks the taboo.

C32.1.1.p: A wife must not see her husband in his transformed, non-human form; seeing him this way breaks the taboo.

C32.1.2.p: A wife breaks the taboo by showing surprise when her supernatural husband returns to his true shape.

C32.2.p: A wife must not question her supernatural husband about who or what he is; asking breaks the taboo.

C32.2.1.p: A wife must not ask the name of her supernatural husband; asking breaks the taboo.

C32.2.2.p: A wife must not ask where her supernatural husband comes from; asking breaks the taboo.

C32.2.3.p: A wife must not ask about the social class or caste of her supernatural husband; asking breaks the taboo.

C32.3.p: A wife must not touch her supernatural husband too soon when he visits her; touching him early breaks the taboo.

C33.p: A supernatural child is a source of taboo; offending against the child breaks a prohibition connected with it.

C33.1.r: (cf. C31.2, C35.1.)—India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 133—136; (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 77ff. No. 12, (Basuto): Jacottet 110; (Ibo of Nigeria): Thomas 76, 80.
C33.1.p: A person must not mention where a supernatural child came from; doing so breaks the taboo.

C35.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 339 n. 223; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 145, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 616.
C35.p: A wife who is an animal, in a tale of an animal-human marriage, breaks a taboo by offending against her animal nature or her husband's rule.

C35.1.r: (Cf. C31.2, C33.1.)—N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 339—342 nn. 222, 223, 233, cf. 234.—Africa (Congo): Weeks 215 No. 11; (Basuto): Jacottet 108 No. 16, (Fjort): Dennett 43 No. 6, (Cameroon): Rosenhuber 44, (Duala): Lederbogen 143.—Indonesian: Dixon 219.
C35.1.p: A person must not mention the origin of their animal wife; doing so breaks the taboo.

C36.p: A taboo: a wife must not offend her animal husband, or he will vanish or be lost to her. The rule is broken and the supernatural spouse is harmed or departs.

C36.1.p: A taboo: a wife must not burn her animal husband's skin or hide. Burning it breaks the bond and the husband leaves or is lost.

C36.2.p: A taboo: a wife must not spy on her animal husband in his true form. Watching him secretly breaks the taboo and the marriage ends.

C37.r: Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 47, 49, (Greenland): Rink 144, (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 156.
C37.p: A taboo: a person must not offend the animal relatives of a supernatural spouse, other than the husband himself. Doing so brings punishment or loss.

C40.p: A taboo: one must not offend the spirits of water, mountains, and similar natural places. Offending them brings harm or punishment.

C41.r: Frazer Golden Bough III 94.—North Carolina: Brown Collection I 641; Africa (Kaffir): Theal 56.
C41.p: A taboo: one must not offend a water-spirit. Doing so brings harm or punishment.

C41.1.p: A taboo: rescuing a drowning man is forbidden, because doing so offends a water-spirit.

C41.2.p: A taboo: letting a ball fall into the water is forbidden, because it offends a water-spirit.

C41.3.p: A taboo: crossing water is forbidden when the water-spirits are offended, since crossing then brings harm.

C41.3.1.p: A taboo: skating over water is forbidden when the water-spirits are offended, since skating counts as crossing and brings harm.

C41.4.p: A taboo: poisoning fish causes a storm, because the water-spirit is offended by it.

C42.p: A taboo: one must not offend a mountain-spirit. Doing so brings harm or punishment.

C43.r: (cf. C51.2.2, C64).—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 295 No. 12; India: Thompson-Balys.
C43.p: A taboo: one must not offend a wood-spirit, or a spirit of the forest. Doing so brings harm or punishment.

C43.1.p: A taboo: one must not offend the spirit of a banyan tree. Doing so brings harm or punishment.

C43.2.p: A taboo: certain trees must not be cut down, because the tree-spirits would be offended.

C43.3.p: A felled tree is restored to standing because the person failed to make the proper offerings to the tree-spirit.

C44.r: Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 321; Herrmann Saxo Gr. II 586.
C44.p: A taboo: one must not offend guardian spirits. Doing so brings harm or punishment.

C45.r: C13). The devil brings the offender into dangerous situation (suspicion of theft or murder), and saves him miraculously when he promises never again to abuse the devil’s likeness. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3325f.; Legends Nos. 631—637, 789; Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges.
C45.p: A taboo: one must not offend the devil. In the tale a smith or priest keeps insulting the devil's statue or picture.

C46.p: A taboo: one must not offend a fairy. Doing so brings harm or punishment.

C46.1.p: A taboo: a promise made to a fairy must not be broken. Breaking it brings death on the twelfth day.

C50.p: A general taboo: breaking a prohibition connected with the gods or supernatural beings brings punishment or misfortune.

C50.1.p: Someone offends the goddess of fortune by breaking a taboo, and suffers bad luck as a result.

C51.p: Handling or touching things belonging to a god is forbidden; doing so is a taboo violation that angers the god.

C51.1.r: Irish myth: Cross, Beal XXI 336; Greek: Grote I 279; India: Thompson-Balys.
C51.1.p: Desecrating or disrespecting a holy place or shrine is forbidden and brings punishment.

C51.1.1.r: Irish: Plummer clxxxiv; Irish myth: Cross.
C51.1.1.p: It is taboo to use a sacred altar for ordinary, everyday purposes.

C51.1.2.r: (Cf. C51.2.)—Fable: Phaedrus IV 11; Wienert FFC LVI 80 (ET 465), 138 (ST 433).
C51.1.2.p: It is taboo to steal from an altar.

C51.1.2.1.p: It is taboo to steal sacred booty, meaning treasure or spoils dedicated to a god.

C51.1.3.r: British: *MacCulloch Celtic 11 (references given to parallels from Parsis, Brahmans, Japanese, and Germans).—Irish myth: Cross.
C51.1.3.p: It is taboo to breathe on the sacred fire.

C51.1.4.p: It is taboo to misuse money placed in a church alms box.

C51.1.5.p: Dancing in a churchyard is taboo and brings punishment.

C51.1.6.p: Stopping the use of a church is a taboo that brings punishment.

C51.1.7.p: Peeping at a sacred baptismal font is taboo.

C51.1.8.p: Letting a drop fall on the altar is a taboo violation.

C51.1.9.p: Unworthy men are forbidden to enter or look upon a sanctuary.

C51.1.10.p: Women are forbidden to enter certain sacred places.

C51.1.11.p: A goddess stops visiting a spring once her sacred spring is disturbed.

C51.1.12.p: Striking a tree that belongs to a deity is taboo and brings punishment.

C51.1.13.p: Treating a goddess's statue or its clothing with scorn is a taboo violation.

C51.1.14.p: Leaving a corpse at a shrine is taboo.

C51.1.15.p: Wearing shoes inside a shrine is taboo.

C51.2.r: (Cf. C51.1.2.)—Greek: Grote I 145; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (3—G 3/1386); S. Am. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 173.
C51.2.p: A taboo against taking or harming things that belong to a god or saint, such as their property or sacred objects.

C51.2.1.r: Crane Liber de Miraculis 82 No. 1; Ward Catalogue of Romances II 603 No. 6, 604 No. 7; Irish saints’ legend: Plummer xliv; Irish myth: Cross.
C51.2.1.p: A taboo against wearing a sacred robe or jewel of a god without permission.

C51.2.2.r: (Cf. C43.)—Irish saints’ legend: Plummer cliii; Irish myth: Cross.
C51.2.2.p: A taboo against cutting down trees or groves that are sacred to a god.

C51.2.2.1.p: A taboo against taking fruit or fish that have been dedicated to a goddess.

C51.2.3.p: A taboo against stealing or taking the wife of a god.

C51.2.4.p: A taboo against stealing from a holy statue or idol.

C51.2.5.p: A taboo against violating a saint's refuge, meaning harming or seizing someone who has sought sanctuary with the saint.

C51.3.r: Jewish: Neuman; Egyptian: Müller 109; Chinese: Werner 294.
C51.3.p: A taboo against revealing or speaking the name of a god.

C51.3.1.p: A taboo against profaning or disrespecting the name of God.

C51.4.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 363 n. 1, Grote I 145.—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 298 No. 6 (investigating secret source of magic wine cask).
C51.4.p: A taboo against revealing or spying on the secrets of a god.

C51.4.1.p: A taboo against intruding on a god's privacy. An emperor, visited by God, hides his wife so she can listen in, and God then stops visiting.

C51.4.2.r: *Toldo Studien zur vgl. Littgsch. IV 52ff.; Irish myth: Cross.
C51.4.2.p: A taboo against spying on the secret help given by angels.

C51.4.3.p: A taboo against spying on the secret help given by fairies.

C51.5.r: Greek: Fox 106 (Salmoneus imitates Zeus’s thunder), Grote I 103f.*, 128; German: Grimm No. 147; India: Thompson-Balys.
C51.5.p: A taboo against imitating a god.

C51.6.r: Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 80 n. 3; Jewish: Neuman.
C51.6.p: A taboo against falsely claiming to have a god's powers.

C51.7.p: A taboo against touching a stone image of a deity with unwashed hands.

C51.8.p: A taboo against giving away an idol.

C51.9.p: A taboo against steering a boat toward the island of the gods.

C52.r: Greek: Fox 46 (Semele in presence of Zeus.)
C52.p: A taboo against being in the presence of a god.

C52.1.p: Speaking directly with a god is deadly for everyone except specially chosen devotees.

C52.2.p: A taboo: a person who suddenly comes upon supernatural creatures while in the presence of a god is punished or harmed for it.

C53.p: A taboo against refusing to give credit to a god: a person who fails to thank or acknowledge God for what they have achieved offends him.

C53.1.p: People whom God taught a craft or skill, but who claim they learned it through their own efforts, and so offend him.

C53.2.p: A taboo against arrogance toward a deity: proud or boastful behavior toward a god is forbidden and brings punishment.

C54.r: Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 20 n. 1 (Thamyris), I 31 (Side), Fox 220 (Marsyas), Grote I 103f., 146, 238, Gaster Thespis 261f., 289; India: Thompson-Balys.
C54.p: A taboo against rivaling the gods: trying to equal or compete with a deity is forbidden and punished.

C55.p: A taboo against losing a consecrated wafer (a holy bread or host): losing or mishandling it offends the divine and brings punishment.

C55.1.p: A taboo against stepping on sacred bread, which is forbidden and offends the divine.

C55.2.r: Type 756C.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3320; Legends Nos. 615—623; Livonian: Loorits in FFC LCVI 59 No. 138.
C55.2.p: A taboo against shooting at a consecrated wafer; the offender is afterward doomed to haunt the earth as a ghost.

C55.3.r: (Cf. B259.4.)—When he dies, his spirit haunts the place. Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 624—627.
C55.3.p: A beekeeper puts a consecrated host into a beehive, and the act is rewarded: his bees thrive.

C56.p: A taboo against behaving improperly while carrying a divine image: unseemly acts during such a procession are forbidden and punished.

C56.1.p: A taboo against defecating while carrying an image of a god, which is forbidden and offends the deity.

C56.2.p: A taboo against stopping along the way while carrying an image of a god; halting on the journey is forbidden and punished.

C57.p: A taboo against neglecting service to a deity: failing to perform the worship or duties owed to a god is forbidden and punished.

C57.1.p: A taboo against neglecting sacrifice to a deity: failing to make the offerings owed to a god is forbidden and punished.

C57.1.1.p: A taboo against fraudulent sacrifice: offering a false or cheating sacrifice to a deity is forbidden and punished.

C57.1.2.p: A taboo that forbids sacrificing to a goddess any man who has a wound.

C57.1.3.p: A taboo against eating from offerings made to gods, which is forbidden and punished.

C57.2.p: A person is punished for refusing to take part in Bacchic (Dionysian wine-god) rites.

C58.r: Irish myth: Cross; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 18 Nos. 163, 166; Hebrew: Exodus 20: 8—11, Neuman; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 390.—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 308 Nos. 37, 38; 324 No. 147; 328 No. 11; India: Thompson-Balys.
C58.p: A taboo against profaning a sacred day: doing forbidden or unholy things on a holy day is punished.

C58.1.p: A taboo against diminishing the number of sacred days, which is forbidden and offends the divine.

C61.p: A taboo against doubting or rejecting religious teachings; breaking it brings punishment.

C61.1.p: A taboo against not believing in God; whoever denies God is punished.

C61.2.p: A taboo against not believing in life after death; doubting immortality is forbidden.

C61.3.p: A taboo against doubting or rejecting sacred scriptures.

C61.4.p: A taboo against disbelieving in a particular supernatural power; doubting it is forbidden.

C62.p: A taboo against worshipping idols or false gods; making or venerating images is forbidden.

C63.r: Greek: Fox 9; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 115; Fiji: Beckwith Myth 138; S. Am. Indian (Witoto): Métraux MAFLS XL 36.
C63.p: A taboo is broken by attacking a god or a sacred person, which brings punishment.

C64.p: A taboo against ignoring a message sent by a god; those who fail to heed it are punished.

C65.p: A taboo against changing a religious ritual or ceremony; altering it is forbidden.

C66.p: A taboo against complaining or grumbling against a god; murmuring against a deity is forbidden.

C67.p: A taboo against letting sacred fires go out or neglecting them.

C68.p: A taboo against failing to keep a vow made to a god; breaking such a promise is forbidden.

C70.p: A taboo against offending sacred beings other than gods, such as spirits or other holy figures.

C71.p: A taboo against disobeying the king; a man who fails to obey the king dies as a result.

C75.p: A taboo against offending the heavenly bodies such as the sun, moon, or stars; offending them is forbidden.

C75.1.r: Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 442, Rasmussen II 25, (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 180.
C75.1.p: A taboo against offending the moon; whoever offends it is punished.

C90.p: Miscellaneous taboos connected with sacred beings that do not fit the other categories.

C91.r: (Cf. C51.2.)—Irish saints’ legend: Plummer cliii (cf. C43, C51.2).—Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 42 No. 53** (cf. C42).
C91.p: A taboo against stealing from spirits; taking things that belong to supernatural beings is forbidden.

C91.1.r: N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 300 n. 96.
C91.1.p: A taboo against stealing a garment from a rock; the offended rock pursues the thief, like a rolling stone chasing him.

C229.5.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat meat and milk together.

C229.6.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat salt.

C230.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat at a certain time.

C230.1.p: A taboo requiring a person to feast for a week.

C231.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat before a certain time has come. Breaking it brings misfortune or punishment.

C231.1.p: A girl is forbidden to eat before her father calls her to the meal. She eats first and suffers for it.

C231.2.p: A person is forbidden to eat until a task is finished. Eating early breaks the taboo.

C231.3.p: A person is forbidden to eat before first offering food to a woman. Eating first breaks the taboo.

C231.3.1.p: A person may not eat a magically caught creature before the mother has eaten it. Eating it first breaks the taboo.

C231.4.p: A host's household may not eat until the house has been set right again. Eating before then breaks the taboo.

C231.5.p: Eight handfuls of food may be eaten only during a ceremony, not at other times.

C231.6.p: A person is forbidden to eat anything until three years have passed.

C232.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat while traveling on a journey. Breaking it brings misfortune.

C232.1.p: A bride is forbidden to eat while travelling to her husband's home. Eating on the journey breaks the taboo.

C234.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat while visiting their home. Breaking it brings misfortune.

C235.p: A taboo forbidding the eating of meat on Maundy Thursday, the Thursday before Easter.

C236.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat after a guest has arrived or been served.

C237.p: A taboo forbidding a feast held by night at the start of the harvest.

C240.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat the food of a certain person. Breaking it brings misfortune.

C241.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat the food of the gods. Breaking it brings punishment.

C241.1.p: A taboo forbidding a person to taste milk from a magical "cow of plenty" that has been dedicated to the gods.

C241.2.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat the chief's food. Breaking it brings punishment.

C243.p: A taboo forbidding a wife to eat the food of her husband after he has been transformed into something else.

C243.1.p: A taboo forbidding a person to eat the food of a supernatural lover. Breaking it brings the lover's loss.

C245.p: A taboo against eating food that birds have already pecked at. Breaking it brings misfortune or punishment on the one who eats.

C246.p: A taboo against eating together with a person of a certain social class or caste. Sharing a meal with such a person is forbidden.

C246.1.p: A taboo under which Jews may not eat with a heathen, that is, a non-Jew.

C246.2.p: A taboo against eating a special food belonging to a noble girl. Anyone who eats it breaks the prohibition.

C247.p: A taboo against eating food that has been placed on a grave. Eating it is forbidden.

C248.p: A taboo against eating food that has been set aside for animals. Eating it is forbidden.

C261.p: A taboo against drinking from a certain fountain or spring.

C262.p: A taboo against drinking in the other world, such as the land of the dead or the otherworld. Drinking there is forbidden.

C263.p: A taboo against drinking from a certain river that flows between two darknesses.

C270.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s. v. “boisson”; Irish myth: Cross.
C270.p: A taboo against drinking certain things. The particular drink forbidden is specified in the subheadings.

C272.1.p: A taboo against drinking wine that has been touched by the hand of a heathen, that is, a non-believer.

C272.2.p: A taboo against drinking wine at a certain time. Drinking it then is forbidden.

C272.3.p: A taboo under which only a prince is allowed to break open a palm-drink (palm wine). Others may not.

C273.p: A taboo against drinking water. The particular water or the time of drinking is specified in the subheadings.

C273.1.p: A taboo against drinking water during a certain time. Drinking it then is forbidden.

C273.2.p: A taboo against drinking water from a certain bottle or flask.

C280.p: A general taboo about eating or drinking that does not fit the more specific eating and drinking categories. Breaking it brings supernatural punishment or misfortune.

C281.p: A taboo against drinking while the dead are not present, so drinking is forbidden unless a dead person is there to join in.

C282.p: A taboo that forbids a person from turning down an invitation to a feast. Refusing brings punishment.

C282.1.p: A taboo that forbids leaving a feast before it has ended. Leaving early brings punishment.

C283.p: A taboo that forbids eating without first giving thanks. Failing to give thanks brings punishment.

C284.p: A taboo that forbids eating alone. Anyone who eats alone breaks it and suffers for it.

C285.p: A taboo that forbids eating in the company of others. Eating together breaks it.

C286.p: A taboo that forbids taking part in a particular feast. Joining that feast breaks it.

C287.p: A taboo that forbids eating a feast before discovering a new wonder or marvel. Eating first breaks it.

C288.p: A taboo that forbids refusing food that has been asked for and provided. Refusing it breaks the taboo.

C311.1.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 50.
C311.1.p: A taboo that forbids looking at supernatural creatures. Seeing such a creature breaks the taboo.

C311.1.1.p: A taboo that forbids looking at ghosts. Seeing a ghost breaks the taboo.

C311.1.2.r: Fb “sygdom” III 699a.—Irish myth: Cross; England, Wales: Baughman.
C311.1.2.p: A taboo that forbids looking at fairies. Seeing a fairy breaks the taboo.

C311.1.3.p: A taboo that forbids looking at mountain-folk, supernatural beings who live in the mountains. Seeing them breaks the taboo.

C311.1.4.p: A taboo that forbids looking at a werewolf. Seeing one in its wolf form breaks the taboo.

C311.1.5.p: A taboo that forbids watching a supernatural helper. Observing the helper breaks the taboo.

C311.1.6.p: A taboo forbids looking at a witch in her true, monstrous form; seeing it breaks the rule.

C311.1.7.p: A taboo forbids looking at game animal that has been killed but has not yet died.

C311.1.8.p: A taboo forbids looking directly at a god.

C311.1.8.1.p: Gods run away or vanish when dawn approaches.

C311.2.p: A taboo forbids looking at holy or sacred objects.

C312.1.p: A taboo forbids a man from looking at a woman who is naked.

C312.1.1.p: A taboo forbids a man from looking at a naked goddess.

C312.1.2.p: A taboo forbids a man from looking at a naked woman who rides through a town.

C312.2.p: A taboo forbids a man from looking at a woman in various other circumstances.

C312.2.2.p: A taboo forbids looking at an old woman helper while she is eating.

C312.2.3.p: A taboo forbids looking at a supernatural woman while she is being dismembered.

C312.2.4.p: A taboo forbids looking at women performing Bacchic (wine-god) rites.

C312.3.p: A man is forbidden to look at his daughter for a long period of twelve years.

C313.p: A taboo forbids a woman from looking at a man.

C313.0.1.p: A princess is forbidden ever to see any male person; all men must hide when she goes out.

C313.1.p: A taboo forbids a woman from seeing a man who is naked.

C313.1.1.p: A goddess is forbidden to see her mortal husband naked.

C315.1.p: A taboo forbids looking at a certain boat; anyone who looks at it breaks the prohibition.

C315.2.p: A taboo forbids looking at a heavenly body such as the sun, moon, or rainbow.

C316.2.p: A taboo forbids looking at a caribou.

C319.1.p: A king is forbidden to look at his own son.

C319.2.p: A taboo against looking at a dead man who was not killed by weapons.

C320.p: A taboo forbids looking into a certain container or receptacle.

C321.2.p: A gift box is opened before the proper time, breaking the prohibition.

C325.p: A taboo against looking into the pots in hell, which are forbidden to be viewed.

C326.p: A taboo against looking under a certain bell before the appointed time.

C327.p: A taboo against looking into a basket.

C426.p: A character is forbidden to reveal or sing a secret song, and breaking the taboo brings harm.

C427.p: A character is forbidden to reveal that a grateful animal has been helping them.

C428.p: A character is forbidden to reveal the time when the Messiah will come.

C429.p: A general prohibition against telling secrets, with punishment or harm following if the taboo is broken.

C429.1.p: A character is forbidden to mention the location of a secret water spring.

C462.p: A taboo against laughing when one sees ghosts; laughing at the sight of spirits breaks the taboo.

C480.p: A general taboo on certain vocal sounds other than speech, such as whistling, singing, weeping or coughing.

C480.1.p: A taboo against whistling; whistling breaks the taboo.

C480.1.1.p: A taboo against whistling in a mine; whistling there breaks the taboo.

C481.1.p: A taboo under which birds may not sing near a goddess's home.

C482.1.p: A taboo under which people in the land of the gods may not weep.

C483.1.p: A taboo against whistling in the other world, such as the land of the dead or spirits.

C484.1.p: A taboo against coughing in the other world, such as the land of the dead or spirits.

C490.p: Miscellaneous taboos on speech that do not fit the other speaking-taboo categories.

C490.1.p: A forbidden expression is replaced by a harmless substitute phrase so that the taboo is not broken.

C490.1.1.p: Instead of the forbidden phrase "save it for tomorrow," people say "save it for the beggar," because tomorrow one may be dead; the substitute avoids the taboo.

C491.r: (Cf. C411, C423.2.)—*Köhler-Bolte I 220.—Irish: Beal XXI 314; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 254 No. 31.
C491.p: A taboo against exclaiming in wonder at something marvelous; a person who does so breaks the prohibition.

C491.1.p: A taboo against screaming when seeing something terrible; the person who screams breaks the prohibition.

C492.p: A taboo against speaking to strangers; breaking it brings trouble.

C493.r: Fb “takke” III 763a; Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 171; Icel.: *Boberg.
C493.p: A taboo against saying thank you, but only under certain circumstances.

C493.1.p: A taboo against wishing someone good luck; for example, one must not wish a hunter good luck or a sailor a good voyage.

C494.p: A taboo against cursing; the person who curses breaks the prohibition.

C495.p: A taboo that allows a person to say anything except one particular phrase.

C495.1.p: A youth is advised by his horse to answer every question with "I don't know" and nothing else.

C495.2.p: Three men speak only the phrases "We three," "For gold," and "That is right," which are their sole conversation.

C495.2.1.p: Three brothers agree to say only the phrases "We three," "For gold," and "That is right"; by speaking them they unwittingly incriminate themselves in a devil's bargain.

C495.2.2.r: *Type 1697; BP II 561; Nouvelles Récréations No. 20; India: Thompson-Balys.
C495.2.2.p: Three travelers each know only one phrase of a foreign language, and by using these phrases they incriminate themselves.

C495.2.2.1.p: A person must not use certain words in a speaking taboo, so they answer with set phrases such as yes, no, or very well, and the phrases here are in a foreign language.

C495.3.p: A youth is advised by an old woman helper to answer every question with "Thanks" and nothing else.

C496.p: A taboo against using obscene or vulgar language; breaking it is forbidden.

C497.p: A taboo against speaking to the dead; breaking it is forbidden.

C498.p: A speaking taboo in which one particular expression is forbidden to be said.

C498.1.p: A speaking taboo in which the forbidden expression is "Sorrow is not eternal."

C499.p: Further speaking taboos that do not fall under the more specific headings.

C499.1.p: A taboo against announcing someone's death directly; the news must not be stated plainly.

C499.2.p: A taboo against paying compliments; praising someone breaks the prohibition.

C500.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “toucher”.—Missouri-French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.
C500.p: A taboo against touching a person or thing; touching it breaks the prohibition.

C501.r: *Frazer Golden Bough@3 III passim.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 95, 98.
C501.p: A taboo against touching or having contact with objects that belong to a king; breaking it brings punishment or misfortune.

C510.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “arbres”.—Jewish: Neuman; Chatham Islands: Beckwith Myth 19, Notes 10, 11, 12.
C510.p: A taboo against touching a tree; the person who touches it is harmed or punished.

C511.p: A taboo against touching the leaves of a tree; touching them brings harm or punishment.

C512.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 181 No. 36.
C512.p: A taboo against picking an ear of grain; doing so is forbidden and brings harm.

C513.r: BP III 62f.; Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Baum”.
C513.p: A taboo against breaking a twig from a tree; doing so is forbidden and brings harm.

C513.1.p: A taboo against cutting off the branches of a tree; doing so is forbidden and brings harm.

C514.p: A taboo against burning saja wood, a particular tree; burning it is forbidden.

C515.r: Type 451; Hartland Science 200.—English-Scottish: Child I 360 n.; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 17.
C515.p: A taboo against touching or picking flowers; doing so is forbidden and brings harm.

C516.r: (Cf. C520.)—English-Scottish: Child V 499 s.v. “trees”—Irish myth: Cross.
C516.p: A taboo against lying down under a tree; a girl who does so is carried off by fairies.

C517.p: A taboo against pulling nuts from a tree; doing so is forbidden and brings harm.

C518.r: Jewish: Neuman; Maori: Clark 95; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z—G 3/1174).
C518.p: A taboo against cutting down a tree; doing so is forbidden and brings harm.

C518.1.p: Cutting down an elder tree is fatal to the man who does it.

C518.2.r: (Cf. C920.) Ireland: Baughman; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn I No. 311, Fb “hvidtjørn” I 703 a.
C518.2.p: Cutting down a white thorn tree is fatal to the man who cuts it.

C519.p: A miscellaneous taboo against touching a tree in various other ways not covered by more specific entries; touching it brings harm.

C519.1.p: A taboo against harming a tree in any way before it is burned; damaging it first is forbidden.

C520.r: (Cf. C516.) Hartland Science 197.—Irish myth: Cross; Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 246; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 303.
C520.p: A taboo against touching the ground; touching it is forbidden and brings harm or punishment.

C521.p: A taboo against getting down from a horse; dismounting is forbidden and brings harm.

C521.1.p: A taboo against getting off a magic sack; dismounting from it is forbidden and brings harm.

C522.r: Fb “plove” II 849b, “höj” I 741b.—Africa (Kaffir): Theal 30 No. 1, 41 No. 2, (Basuto): Jacottet 100 No. 15, (Zulu): Callaway 99, (Yoruba): Ellis 253 No. 4.
C522.p: A taboo against plowing in a certain place; plowing there is forbidden and brings harm.

C523.r: (Cf. C522.)—N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 332 n. 197.
C523.p: A taboo against digging in the ground; digging is forbidden and brings harm.

C523.1.p: A taboo forbids digging up certain stones; breaking it brings a penalty. The prohibition is about disturbing particular stones in the ground.

C523.2.p: A taboo forbids digging inside a fairy ring, the circle of mushrooms or grass associated with fairies. Digging there breaks the prohibition.

C524.p: A taboo forbids a person who has returned from the otherworld or fairyland from setting foot on land as soon as they leave the boat. Stepping ashore breaks the prohibition.

C525.p: A taboo forbids picking up a card that has fallen to the ground. Doing so breaks the prohibition.

C526.p: A taboo forbids touching a sacred mountain. Setting hands or feet on it breaks the prohibition.

C530.p: A general heading for taboos about touching various things. The entries below it name specific objects or beings that must not be touched.

C531.r: *MacCulloch Childhood 339; Hartland Science 163f.; Fb “jærn” II 61a.—Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Holm 93.
C531.p: A taboo forbids touching iron. Contact with iron breaks the prohibition.

C531.1.p: A taboo forbids cutting an umbilical cord with iron, so the cord must be severed by some other means.

C532.p: A taboo forbids touching water. Contact with water breaks the prohibition.

C533.p: A taboo forbids touching a box. Touching it breaks the prohibition.

C533.1.r: (Cf. D1174.) Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 18, 178, (Vai): Ellis 187 No. 3, (Basuto): Jacottet 220 No. 33.
C533.1.p: A taboo forbids touching a magic box, a special container with supernatural powers. Touching it breaks the prohibition.

C535.p: A taboo forbids stepping on bread or otherwise mistreating it. Misusing bread breaks the prohibition.

C536.p: A taboo forbids cleaning houses with cow dung. Doing so breaks the prohibition.

C537.p: A general heading for taboos about touching certain animals. The entries below name specific animals that must not be touched.

C537.1.p: A taboo forbids touching a camel after it has retired from work. Touching it then breaks the prohibition.

C537.2.p: A taboo forbids touching a hairless dog. Touching it breaks the prohibition.

C537.3.p: A taboo forbids touching a horse, or touching a dead cat or dog while moving it. Doing so breaks the prohibition.

C541.p: A taboo forbids contact with the dead. Touching a corpse or dead person breaks the prohibition.

C541.1.p: A taboo forbids having a dead body on a ship. Carrying a corpse aboard breaks the prohibition.

C541.2.p: A taboo forbids moving the head of a slain man. Moving it breaks the prohibition.

C541.3.p: A taboo against touching the bones of a person who was murdered. Breaking it brings supernatural trouble.

C541.4.p: A taboo against lying down on the bones of one's ancestors.

C541.5.p: A taboo against taking down the body of a man who has been hanged. Breaking it is forbidden.

C541.6.p: A taboo against embalming a dead body, meaning preserving it after death.

C542.r: *Krappe Balor 125 n. 17.—Icel.: Herrmann Saxo II 589; MacCulloch Eddic 321, *Boberg.
C542.p: A taboo against touching the treasures belonging to the other world, such as the dead's possessions there.

C542.1.p: A taboo against touching certain things met on the journey to hell or the underworld.

C542.2.r: S. Am. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 45.
C542.2.p: A taboo against touching fire in the other world, the land of the dead.

C543.p: A taboo against picking up a comb from the ground. The comb belongs to a fairy or witch, who will take revenge for the insult.

C544.1.p: A taboo against crushing the eggs of a lizard.

C545.p: A taboo against touching certain kinds of clothing.

C545.1.p: A taboo against touching old clothes. Abandoned clothes should be thrown away rather than handled.

C545.2.p: A taboo against touching the clothes of a certain person.

C545.3.p: A taboo against touching a dress.

C546.p: A taboo against striking a certain rock.

C549.p: A general taboo against touching something, where the specific object is not named.

C549.1.p: After killing a man, a tiger or lion is forbidden to touch certain animals: cow, buffalo, pig, deer, or wild goat.

C549.1.1.p: A taboo against touching a horse, or moving a dead cat or dog. This is one form of the tiger and lion taboo on touching certain animals after killing a man.

C549.2.p: A taboo against touching the soldiers of an enchanted, sleeping army or their horses.

C550.p: A taboo that applies to an entire class or group of people, not just one individual.

C551.p: Certain castes or social groups are regarded as untouchable, because contact with them is believed to pollute others.

C551.1.p: A taboo forbids a person from touching or eating food that belongs to a member of a different caste, under pain of pollution or punishment.

C560.p: A general heading for taboos that bar certain social classes from doing particular things that are permitted to others.

C561.p: Restrictions that apply to slaves, forbidding them to do things that free people may do.

C561.1.r: African (Ekoi): Talbot 27; Maori: Clark 128; Jewish: Neuman.
C561.1.p: A slave is forbidden to go near a fetish, a sacred object believed to hold magical power.

C563.p: Restrictions placed on kings, forbidding them to do certain things that ordinary people may do.

C563.1.p: A king must not travel alone.

C563.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: *Neuman.
C563.2.p: A king is forbidden to have any physical blemish or bodily defect.

C563.3.p: A king must not allow plunder or rape to occur during his reign.

C563.4.p: A king must not settle a quarrel between thralls, that is, between unfree servants.

C563.5.p: A person must not appear before the king unless the king has summoned them.

C563.6.p: No one may kill the king, even if the king himself asks to be killed.

C564.p: Restrictions placed on chiefs, forbidding them to do certain things that others may do.

C564.1.p: A chief must not sit in an ale-house when no story-telling is going on.

C564.2.p: A chief's troop must not be without a herald.

C564.3.p: A chief must not appear in a large company without wolfhounds with him.

C564.4.p: Cloth made from a certain bark is forbidden to everyone except chiefs.

C564.5.p: Smoke from a sacrifice on the altar must not touch a young chief.

C564.6.p: Commoners are forbidden to be taught the genealogy of chiefs.

C564.7.r: Hawaii, Marquesas, Lau Islands: Beckwith Myth 468.
C564.7.p: No one may touch the head of a chief.

C564.8.p: A chieftainess is forbidden to prepare food herself. Breaking this taboo brings misfortune or punishment.

C564.9.p: A chief is forbidden to go outdoors even when provoked or insulted. He must stay inside rather than respond.

C565.p: Bearded men are subject to a set of taboos, forbidding them certain actions.

C565.1.p: A bearded man is forbidden to do manual labor. Doing so breaks the taboo.

C565.2.p: A bearded man is forbidden to be lazy or idle. Idleness breaks the taboo.

C566.p: Heroes are bound by a set of taboos, forbidding them certain actions or situations.

C566.1.p: A fish-hero must not catch a certain being in the bays of his own land. Doing so breaks the taboo.

C566.2.p: Birds may not feed on the hero's land unless they leave him something. Taking food without leaving a share breaks the taboo.

C566.3.p: Women may not leave the hero's land without his knowing it. Leaving secretly breaks the taboo.

C566.4.p: Women may not marry until the hero has chosen their husbands for them.

C566.5.p: Warriors may not be in the hero's land without first receiving a challenge from him. Entering without one breaks the taboo.

C566.6.p: Warriors are forbidden to have sexual activity. Breaking this taboo is the violation.

C567.p: Princesses are bound by a set of taboos, forbidding them certain actions.

C567.1.p: A man may not elope with the king's daughter. Doing so breaks the taboo.

C567.2.p: A princess must not step into water. Doing so breaks the taboo.

C568.p: Poets are bound by a set of taboos, forbidding them certain actions.

C568.1.p: Poets must not know their nation's literature. Knowing it breaks the taboo.

C572.p: A thief is bound by a set of taboos, forbidding him certain actions.

C573.p: Priests are bound by a set of taboos, forbidding them certain actions.

C575.p: Illegitimate children are bound by a set of taboos, forbidding them certain actions.

C576.p: A taboo, or ban, on certain things that people of a particular social class or status may not do.

C600.r: Celtic: *Schoepperle Tristan and Isolt. II 307.—Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
C600.p: A person is forbidden to do one particular thing, while being free to do everything else.

C601.p: A single forbidden act is announced to a person by a mysterious or unseen voice.

C610.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “interdits”.—Irish myth: Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys; Jewish: *Neuman; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 86; Africa (Luba): DeClerq Zs. f. KS. IV 219; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 70, 186; Marquesas: Handy 36; New Hebrides: Codrington 385; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z—G 13/317).
C610.p: One particular place is forbidden to enter, while all other places are open.

C611.r: Types 311, 312, 313, 314, 480, 502, 516, 710; *BP I 21; *Cox Cinderella 484; Roberts* (Type 480) 174.—*MacCulloch Childhood 306; *Chauvin V 302 No. 117; **Hartland FLJ III 193; Fb “kammer” II 83, “menneske” II 577b; Penzer II 223 n. 1, 252f., VII 21 n. 3, VIII 57 n. 1; Rösch FFC LXXVII 98; Clouston Tales I 198ff.; Köhler-Bolte I 129, 312.—Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 101; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “chambre”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 23; Missouri French: Carrière; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 304 No. 30; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Spanish Exempla: Keller.—Seneca: Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 135 No. 21; Tonga: Gifford 189.
C611.p: A person may enter every room of a house except one, which is forbidden.

C611.1.r: *Kirby FLJ V 112; *Chauvin V 203 No. 117; India: Thompson-Balys; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 275 No. 86; Seneca: Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 75 No. 1.
C611.1.p: A person may pass through every door except one, which is forbidden to open.

C611.1.1.p: A prince is not to be given the eighth key until he has ruled for five years.

C611.2.p: A person may go everywhere except into three particular stables, which are forbidden.

C611.3.p: A particular ladder is forbidden to climb, while everything else is allowed.

C612.r: (Cf. C614.1.0.2.)—Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 142; African (Pahouini): Largeau 195, (Bondei): Woodward FL XXXVI 367ff. No. 12.
C612.p: One particular forest is forbidden to enter, while other places are open.

C614.p: All roads may be taken except one, which is forbidden.

C614.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
C614.1.p: A person may not travel in one particular direction, but is free to go in any other.

C614.1.0.1.p: A taboo against traveling in a certain direction while herding cattle.

C614.1.0.2.p: A taboo against hunting in a certain part of a forest.

C614.1.0.3.p: A person must not step outside a certain line or boundary.

C614.1.3.p: A taboo forbidding a person to travel or go in the direction of west.

C614.1.5.p: Traveling toward either sunset or sunrise is forbidden.

C614.2.p: A taboo against going through a wicket gate, a small gate.

C615.p: A body of water such as a lake or pool that the hero or others are forbidden to enter or go near.

C615.1.p: A lake or pool that is forbidden to visit or approach.

C615.2.p: The hero is forbidden to swim in a certain lake.

C615.3.p: A lake may not be visited at a certain time of day or year.

C615.4.p: It is taboo to rest or camp beside a lake.

C615.5.p: A certain pool may only be approached if one is dressed in the proper clothing.

C616.p: A visitor who is feasted at a certain place must not be allowed to eat there, as a taboo.

C617.p: A country that the hero or others are forbidden to enter.

C617.1.p: A ford, a shallow crossing of a river, that is forbidden and dangerous to cross.

C619.p: Miscellaneous forbidden places that do not fit other categories.

C619.1.p: An inn or lodging place that is forbidden to enter or stay in.

C619.2.p: It is taboo to go into the haunt or lair of a wild boar.

C619.3.p: A horse fair that is forbidden to attend.

C619.4.p: Women are forbidden to set foot on a certain island.

C620.p: A taboo in which a person must not eat or partake of one particular forbidden object, while everything else is allowed.

C621.r: *Frazer Testament I 45ff.; *Dh I 208ff.—Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 381ff.; Burmese, Indo-Chinese: Scott Indo-Chinese 265, 289.—N. A. Indian (Biloxi): Dorsey and Swanton RBAE XLVII 32; (Quiché): Alexander Lat. Am. 171; S. Am. Indian (Yuracare): ibid. 315.
C621.p: A tree whose fruit may be eaten from all trees except this one, which is forbidden.

C621.1.p: The tree of knowledge is forbidden to eat from.

C621.2.p: It is taboo even to touch the fruit of a certain tree.

C621.2.1.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. *”Apfel” n. 31.—Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 41 No. 301.
C621.2.1.p: It is taboo even to touch an apple.

C621.2.2.p: It is taboo even to touch a banana.

C622.p: A drinking horn that the character is forbidden to drink from; drinking from any other vessel is allowed. Breaking the prohibition brings trouble.

C623.r: (One may not go there unless accompanied by cup-bearers.) Irish myth: Cross.
C623.p: A well that the character is forbidden to draw from or approach. It is the one forbidden object in the tale, and touching or using it brings punishment.

C623.1.p: A well so dangerous that anyone who looks into it loses his eyes.

C624.p: A barrel that the character is forbidden to open or drink from. It is the one forbidden object in the tale, and disobedience brings trouble.

C625.p: A bottle that the character is forbidden to open. Opening it is the taboo, and breaking it brings consequences.

C630.p: A particular time or day on which a certain action is forbidden. Everything else at other times is permitted.

C631.r: Hebrew: Exodus 20; 8—12.—Jewish: *Neuman; Irish myth: Cross; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 17f. Nos. 157—170.
C631.p: Breaking the Sabbath, that is, doing forbidden work on the holy day of rest. Specific Sabbath prohibitions are listed beneath it.

C631.1.r: Jewish: *Neuman; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
C631.1.p: Travelling or journeying on the Sabbath, which is forbidden.

C631.2.p: Spinning thread or yarn on a holy day, which is forbidden.

C631.3.p: Washing one's hair on the Sabbath, which is forbidden.

C631.4.p: Lighting or putting out lamps or fires on the Sabbath, which is forbidden.

C631.5.p: Writing anything on the Sabbath, which is forbidden.

C631.6.p: Playing music on the Sabbath, which is forbidden.

C632.p: Going out of one's home or country on Hallowe'en, which is forbidden.

C634.p: Eating no food or fasting on certain holidays is forbidden.

C635.p: Giving a ring at a certain time is forbidden.

C636.p: Hunting is forbidden on the shortest day of the year, the winter solstice.

C640.p: A miscellaneous prohibition that is unique to the tale and does not fit the other categories of forbidden things, times or objects.

C641.p: It is forbidden to make war against a certain tribe or people. Going to war against them brings punishment or misfortune.

C641.1.p: It is forbidden to make war against a certain tribe specifically on a Tuesday.

C642.p: A taboo in which a person must not make peace with a particular tribe or people; breaking it brings trouble.

C643.p: A taboo against turning the left side of a chariot toward a certain place; doing so is forbidden.

C644.p: The one forbidden thing is to return to one's home country after marrying a fairy; breaking this rule ends the happiness.

C650.r: **Reinhard the Survival of Geis in Mediaeval Romance.—Irish myth: Cross, MacCulloch Celtic 177ff., passim, *Schoepperle Tristan and Isolt II 307; Beal XXI 312.
C650.p: A person must do one specific thing, or misfortune will come; sometimes the doing is forced by magic.

C650.1.p: Customs that are tied to a single thing a person is compelled to do.

C651.r: Voretzsch Altfranz Lit. 325 (Chretien de Troyes Conte del Graal).
C651.p: A person must ask the meaning of the strange sights he sees, or a king will not be healed; the question is required to cure him.

C652.p: A hero must take back a talisman that opened a treasure mountain, but he takes the treasure and forgets the talisman.

C655.p: Only one particular gift may be accepted; any other gift is refused.

C655.1.p: Only the peacock on top of the king's golden temple steeple may be accepted as a dowry.

C661.p: A girl from fairyland must eat earthly food in order to stay on earth.

C662.p: A person must eat a certain poisonous vegetable called the death vegetable whenever he sees it, or a god will be angry.

C663.p: A person is compelled to bathe daily in certain waters.

C664.p: A person must marry the first woman he meets.

C664.0.1.p: A man must sleep with the first woman he meets after a battle.

C665.p: A person must protect a certain stone from being touched or disturbed.

C666.p: A person must go to a certain place at a certain time, or once every year.

C671.p: Beer may not be brewed until an old man sings the song of how beer began.

C672.p: A person is compelled to tell stories.

C672.1.p: A man who fails to tell the stories he is bound to tell is cursed: the stories creep out of his belly while he sleeps and talk.

C675.p: A person must give food to everyone he meets on a journey.

C680.p: A general heading for other strange compulsions in which a person is bound to do one particular thing, usually under threat of misfortune.

C681.p: The hero is magically forced to answer a call or cry, whether he wants to or not.

C681.1.p: A magical compulsion to heed the cry of a hunt and to follow the hunting hounds.

C682.p: A person must invite a singer to a feast, and until this is done the beer keeps foaming and will not settle.

C683.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 213 No. 73.
C683.p: A command to sleep wherever night finds you, since otherwise misfortune will follow.

C684.p: A person is compelled to carry out a particular task every year.

C684.1.p: A yearly compulsion to catch a blackbird alive.

C684.2.p: A yearly compulsion to kill one of a certain group of hogs.

C684.3.p: A yearly compulsion to leap over a stone that is as big as one's own body, held in the palm of the hand.

C684.4.p: A compulsion to hold a festival at set intervals.

C685.p: A command to give a sample of food to a dog before eating, since failing to do so brings misfortune.

C686.p: A command to abandon a woman who stirs up love in a man, presumably to avoid harm.

C686.1.p: A taboo forbidding a person to help a woman.

C687.p: A command to perform a particular act every day.

C687.1.p: A command to visit a saint every day.

C700.p: A general heading for taboos that do not fit the more specific categories in the index.

C710.r: Babylonian: Gilgamesch-Epos XII p. 64ff.—Icelandic: Boberg; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 371, 440, Rasmussen III 170; Marquesas: Beckwith Myth 149.
C710.p: A general heading for taboos that apply to journeys into the other world, such as the realm of spirits or fairies.

C711.p: A taboo that requires a person returning from the serpent kingdom to go into a bath.

C712.p: A taboo against staying too long in the other world; lingering there brings harm or consequences.

C712.1.r: (Cf. C713.3.)—*R. M. Meyer Zs. f. Vksk. XXI 1ff.
C712.1.p: A taboo against staying too long in fairyland.

C713.r: Tabu: association of fairy’s (merman’s, etc.) human wife (husband) with human relatives.
C713.p: A merman or other supernatural husband is left behind by his human wife, who has broken a taboo tied to his otherworld origin. The motif covers the forsaken spouse as a whole.

C713.1.p: A merman's wife must not stay until the church blessing; if she does, she loses him or breaks the bond.

C713.2.r: Usually a part of the “Star-Husband” tale of the North American Indians: Thompson Tales 332 n. 197.
C713.2.p: The wife of a supernatural husband must not visit her old home; going back to see it breaks the taboo.

C713.3.p: A merman's wife must not stay too long when visiting her own people, or the bond with her husband is broken.

C713.3.1.p: When a beast-husband is kept waiting too long because his wife stays away on a visit, he falls sick.

C713.4.p: A golden apple is thrown to remind the merman's wife to return to him, as a sign not to forget her way back.

C714.p: Rules about what may be asked for when visiting the otherworld, such as limits on the number of gifts or favours requested.

C714.1.p: When visiting the home of a spirit son-in-law, only one gift may be asked for.

C715.p: A general taboo against speaking while in the otherworld; speaking there breaks the rule.

C715.1.p: A person must not speak while in fairyland; speaking there breaks the taboo.

C715.2.p: A person must not make noise on the way to the otherworld; making a noise breaks the taboo.

C716.p: A taboo against taking off one's hat while in the otherworld; removing it breaks the rule.

C720.p: A general taboo concerning the performing of bodily functions, such as going to the toilet.

C721.p: A taboo against bathing; bathing breaks the rule.

C721.1.p: A taboo that forbids bathing at certain times; bathing at the forbidden time breaks it.

C721.2.p: A taboo that forbids bathing in certain places; bathing in the forbidden place breaks it.

C721.2.1.p: A taboo that allows bathing only in a clear stream; bathing in a murky or other water breaks the rule.

C721.3.p: A taboo against bathing without afterwards straining the stream, meaning one must clear or strain the water after bathing.

C722.p: A taboo against cutting one's hair; cutting it breaks the rule.

C722.0.1.p: A taboo against shaving; shaving breaks the rule.

C722.1.p: Cutting one's hair at a particular time is forbidden.

C723.1.p: Combing one's hair is forbidden at a certain time.

C725.p: Going to relieve oneself at a certain time is forbidden.

C725.1.p: Using water after relieving oneself is forbidden.

C726.1.p: Throwing away one's nail trimmings is forbidden.

C730.p: Taking rest or stopping to rest is forbidden.

C731.p: Resting while on a journey is forbidden.

C735.1.p: Sleeping at a certain time is forbidden.

C735.1.0.1.p: Sleeping in a certain position at a certain time is forbidden.

C735.1.1.p: A bearded man must not sleep at sunrise.

C735.1.2.p: Sleeping before a task is finished is forbidden.

C735.2.p: Sleeping in a certain place is forbidden.

C735.2.1.p: Sleeping in the other world is forbidden.

C735.2.1.1.p: In cloudland one must not sleep before seven days have passed.

C735.2.2.p: Sleeping in an empty hut is forbidden.

C735.2.3.p: A king or hero must not sleep after sunrise at the capital.

C735.2.4.p: Sleeping in a house that is lit after sunset is forbidden.

C735.2.5.p: A taboo against sleeping in a cemetery. Breaking it brings danger or misfortune.

C735.2.6.p: A taboo against sleeping where ghosts walk. Anyone who sleeps on their path breaks the rule.

C735.2.7.p: A taboo against sleeping on a feather bed.

C735.2.8.p: A taboo against sleeping two nights in the same place. The person must move on until a certain result is reached.

C735.2.9.p: A taboo against resting, either sitting or lying down, until someone learns the answer to a certain question.

C735.2.10.p: A taboo against sleeping in one's own home.

C740.p: A taboo against doing a kindly deed, such as an act of mercy or courtesy, when the rule forbids it.

C741.p: A taboo against freeing or relieving the souls suffering in hell. A boy who tends the kettles there may not lift the lids to ease the poor souls.

C742.p: A taboo against striking a monster a second time. Although the monster begs to be struck again, the hero refuses, because a second blow would bring the monster back to life.

C742.1.p: A man can be killed only by the first blow. After that, others cannot harm him.

C743.p: A taboo against putting one's house in order for a single man, a rule that forbids tidying up for just one person.

C744.p: A taboo against accepting an invitation.

C745.p: A taboo against entertaining or taking in strangers.

C745.1.p: A taboo against heeding an old woman's pleas for food and warmth. The old woman turns out to be a transformed demon.

C746.p: A taboo against watching a game without helping the player who is losing.

C747.p: A taboo against letting any other creature onto a raft.

C751.p: A taboo against doing a certain thing at a certain time.

C761.2.p: A taboo against staying too long at home. Lingering there brings misfortune.

C761.3.p: A taboo against staying too long at a ball or dance. The person must leave before a set hour.

C761.4.p: A taboo against staying too long in one particular place.

C761.4.3.p: An angel is forbidden to remain on earth for more than one week.

C762.p: A general taboo against repeating an activity too often. Doing it too frequently brings punishment or misfortune.

C762.4.p: A taboo against picking more than one fruit from a certain tree.

C762.5.p: A man is allowed to take money from a cursed chest only twice, and no more.

C766.p: A taboo against eating more after one is already full. Continuing to eat past satisfaction is forbidden.

C766.1.p: A taboo against killing more cattle than one can eat. Slaughtering surplus animals is forbidden.

C770.p: A general taboo against overweening pride, meaning arrogant or excessive self-confidence.

C770.1.p: A man is forbidden to be proud of his good fortune, since he and his clan have never known unhappiness or want. Such pride is punished by the earth swallowing them up.

C771.p: A taboo against building a structure that is too large. Overly grand building is forbidden.

C771.1.p: A taboo against building a tower that is too high.

C773.p: A taboo against wanting more power than is proper. Reaching for too much authority or control is forbidden.

C773.1.1.p: A taboo against asking for an excessively large magical multiplication of coins. Asking for too much money from a magic source is forbidden.

C776.p: A taboo against counting one's possessions. Doing so is forbidden.

C780.p: A general taboo against buying, selling, or giving things in certain ways or under certain conditions.

C782.1.p: A taboo against selling used clothing.

C782.2.p: A taboo against selling something to a witch.

C783.1.p: A taboo against giving away a certain kind of money.

C783.2.p: A taboo against giving away rings.

C784.p: A general taboo against lending things, under the conditions stated.

C784.1.p: A taboo against lending things to a witch.

C785.p: A taboo against trying to save food or supplies for later. Hoarding provisions for another day is forbidden.

C810.p: A general taboo against heeding a persuasive person or thing, meaning listening to or obeying someone or something that tempts.

C811.p: A taboo against listening to persuasive voices that tempt one to act against the prohibition.

C811.1.r: Roberts Type 480, p. 204; Benga: Nassau No. 11.
C811.1.p: A taboo against picking up a magic drum that calls out "take me." The drum's persuasive voice must not be obeyed.

C811.2.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 90 No. 16.
C811.2.p: A taboo: a magic yam warns the person not to dig it up, and breaking this prohibition brings trouble. The person is tempted to take it anyway.

C811.3.p: A taboo: the person must not answer a call made while they are asleep, because answering brings harm.

C812.p: A taboo: the person must not chase or pursue a certain animal.

C815.p: A taboo: the person must not follow their mother's advice. Disobeying or obeying the forbidden counsel brings trouble.

C815.1.p: A taboo: the person must not follow the advice of a princess, and doing so is forbidden.

C820.p: A taboo: the person must not discover a certain secret. Learning it is forbidden.

C821.p: A taboo: the person must not find out how old a monster is.

C822.p: A taboo: the person solves a sphinx's riddle and the sphinx dies as a result.

C824.p: A taboo: the person must not learn the name of a ghost.

C825.p: A taboo: the person must not study forbidden or occult books.

C832.p: A taboo: the person must not spin thread or yarn.

C836.p: A taboo against disobeying; here, all guests must obey their host without question.

C837.p: A taboo against loosing the bridle when selling a man who has been transformed into a horse.

C841.6.p: A taboo against killing a golden duck.

C841.11.p: A taboo against killing a cat.

C901.4.p: Whoever sets a punishment for breaking a taboo is himself caught by that same penalty when he breaks it.

C901.4.1.p: A king breaks the taboo he himself set and suffers the punishment he had decreed for it. In the tale his nose is cut off.

C905.p: A supernatural being punishes someone who breaks a taboo.

C905.1.p: A dwarf punishes a person for breaking a taboo.

C905.2.p: The moon punishes a person for breaking a taboo.

C910.p: A person who breaks a taboo is marked with a permanent sign of their disobedience.

C911.r: (Cf. C611.)—*Type 710; BP I 21 (Grimm Nos 3, 136).—Missouri French: Carrière.
C911.p: A person who opens a forbidden room or chamber is left with a golden finger as a lasting sign.

C912.r: (Cf. C611.)—*Types 314, 480; Fb “hår” I 771b; German: Grimm No. 136; Roberts Type 480 p. 174.
C912.p: A person who enters a forbidden room is punished by having their hair turn to gold, a lasting mark of the disobedience.

C913.p: A key is stained with blood after its owner has disobeyed a prohibition, showing the disobedience.

C913.1.p: An egg turns bloody as a visible sign that a forbidden thing was touched or disobeyed.

C915.p: Something kept inside a forbidden container is let out when someone breaks the prohibition and opens it.

C915.1.r: See references to C321 (Tabu: looking into box).
C915.1.p: When a forbidden casket is opened, troubles or evils fly out into the world.

C915.1.1.r: Köhler’s notes to Gonzenbach Sicilianische Märchen No. 15.
C915.1.1.p: A music box keeps playing after it is touched against a prohibition, and cannot be stopped.

C915.2.p: When forbidden baskets are opened, animals come out and escape.

C915.2.1.p: When a forbidden calabash (gourd container) is opened, animals escape from it.

C916.p: Breaking a prohibition sets off an action that goes on continuously without stopping.

C916.1.p: A candle left dripping reveals that someone has trespassed where they were forbidden to go.

C916.2.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 90, No. 16.
C916.2.p: Animals keep appearing out of a forbidden drum each time it is beaten.

C916.3.p: A magic porridge pot keeps cooking and filling the house, because a command to stop was not obeyed by the person who had been told not to use it. It stops only when its mistress orders it to.

C916.4.p: A spinning wheel keeps turning on its own because a woman used it at a time she was forbidden to work.

C917.p: Something appears out of nothing as soon as a prohibition is broken.

C917.1.p: When a forbidden pot is broken, a whole town appears in its place.

C918.p: A magic mare from the water world vanishes when she is scolded and her halter is put to ordinary use.

C918.1.p: A marvelous cow vanishes after it has been offended.

C920.p: The person who breaks the prohibition is put to death.

C921.p: A person who breaks a taboo (a forbidden act) is killed on the spot.

C922.p: A man is given a secret box with the power to make women love him, ignores a warning and opens it, and the women smother him to death.

C922.1.p: A person dies by choking as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C924.p: A person who breaks a taboo is punished by dying of thirst.

C925.p: A person who breaks a taboo dies from a rattlesnake bite.

C926.r: Calif Indian: Gayton and Newman 100; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 147.
C926.p: A man or woman disappears when a taboo is broken.

C927.3.p: A person who breaks a taboo is punished by being both burned and drowned.

C928.p: A person who breaks a taboo goes insane and dies as punishment.

C929.2.1.p: A person dies of paralysis as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C929.3.p: A person who breaks a taboo is beheaded.

C929.4.p: A person who breaks a taboo is stoned to death.

C929.5.p: A person who breaks a taboo is swallowed by a creature.

C929.6.p: A man is sacrificed to the gods as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C933.2.p: Breaking a taboo causes a person to lose their luck in fishing.

C934.r: Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 452, (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 200; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 111; Samoa: ibid. 450.
C934.p: Breaking a taboo causes the food supply to fail, so there is not enough to eat.

C934.1.p: Breaking a taboo causes the crops to fail.

C934.2.p: Breaking a taboo causes the land to become barren and unable to grow anything.

C934.3.p: Because a taboo was broken, elves set the country on fire.

C935.r: *Fb “spise” III 495e; Hartland Science 142; Irish: Beal XXI 329, 337; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 245.
C935.p: A helpful animal vanishes once a taboo is broken.

C936.p: A army loses a war because a taboo was broken.

C937.r: (Cf. C621.)—Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Tahiti: Henry 85; New Hebrides: Codrington 387; African (Ekoi): Talbot 129.
C937.p: A person loses God's favor as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C937.1.p: Breaking a taboo causes a person to lose immortality.

C938.p: After a taboo is broken, the rulers become people of inferior character.

C939.p: Miscellaneous punishments in which a broken taboo brings loss of fortune.

C939.1.p: Because a taboo was broken, water is withdrawn from a lake.

C939.2.p: Because a taboo was broken, good money turns into counterfeit money.

C939.3.p: Because a taboo was broken, felled trees or cut weeds return to their original places.

C941.1.p: A person who breaks a taboo is afflicted with leprosy.

C941.2.p: A person's limbs swell up as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C941.3.p: Sores break out over the body as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C941.3.1.p: The mouth becomes sore as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C941.4.p: A plague strikes as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C941.5.r: African (Luba): De Clerq Zs. f. KS. IV 220.
C941.5.p: A person is paralyzed as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C942.r: Irish myth: Cross; Danish: Fb “klæder” II 200a.
C942.p: A person loses strength or magical power because a taboo was broken.

C942.1.p: Smoking causes a person to lose magical strength, because it breaks a taboo.

C942.2.p: A magic horse loses its powers after someone breaks a taboo.

C942.3.p: A man becomes weak after seeing a naked woman who is a fairy.

C942.4.p: A woman's breasts dry up as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C943.2.p: A person loses one eye as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C943.3.p: A person's eyes become sore as punishment for breaking a taboo.

C944.p: A person who breaks a tabu (a forbidden act) is punished by being made unable to speak.

C946.3.p: A person who breaks a tabu has body parts grow abnormally, by magic, as punishment.

C947.p: A person who breaks a tabu loses their magic power.

C948.4.p: A man's liver is snatched away as punishment for breaking a tabu.

C948.5.p: A man's lungs are cut out as punishment for breaking a tabu.

C948.6.p: A person who breaks a tabu has a hand cut off as punishment.

C948.7.p: A person's face becomes chilled as punishment for breaking a tabu.

C948.8.p: A person's head is shattered as punishment for breaking a tabu.

C949.p: Miscellaneous sicknesses or weaknesses that befall a person as punishment for breaking a tabu.

C949.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Icel.: Boberg.
C949.1.p: A person who breaks a tabu becomes insane.

C949.2.p: A person who breaks a tabu goes bald.

C949.3.p: A person who breaks a tabu becomes sterile and cannot have children.

C949.4.p: A person who breaks a taboo starts bleeding as a punishment.

C984.3.p: A flood covers the land as punishment for breaking a taboo.
